items.a_text: It is unclear to what extent nudging interventions can be transparent without losing effectiveness.
items.b_text: Conditions making a nudge easy and cheap to avoid, specifically transparency and deliberation-triggering, are often violated.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the empirical uncertainty regarding whether transparency reduces the effectiveness of nudges, whereas Claim B observes that real-world nudges frequently fail to implement transparency.

items.a_text: Compelling new hires to make active decisions about 401(k) enrollment raises the initial fraction that enroll by 28 percentage points relative to a standard opt-in enrollment procedure.
items.b_text: A substantial fraction of 401(k) participants hired under automatic enrollment retain the default contribution rate.
items.explanation: The claims examine distinct choice architecture mechanisms within 401(k) plans, with one focusing on active decision enrollment rates and the other on default stickiness under automatic enrollment.

items.a_text: Nudge interventions can be conceptually categorized into three degrees based on their impact on individual decision-making autonomy.
items.b_text: An alternative framework classifies nudges into two categories: Type 1 and Type 2.
items.explanation: The claims propose two distinct categorization frameworks for nudges based on different criteria without mutually confirming or refuting each other.

items.a_text: Compelling new hires to make active decisions about 401(k) enrollment raises the initial fraction that enroll by 28 percentage points relative to a standard opt-in enrollment procedure.
items.b_text: 401(k) participation is significantly higher under automatic enrollment.
items.explanation: Although both claims concern mechanisms for increasing 401(k) participation, they evaluate distinct interventions—active choice versus automatic enrollment—and therefore do not directly support or contradict one another.

items.a_text: It is unclear to what extent nudging interventions can be transparent without losing effectiveness.
items.b_text: Transparent default nudges do not diminish their effectiveness and can in some cases enhance compliance.
items.explanation: Claim A highlights general uncertainty about whether transparent nudging reduces effectiveness, whereas Claim B provides a specific empirical finding that transparent default nudges maintain or enhance effectiveness.

items.a_text: Compelling new hires to make active decisions about 401(k) enrollment raises the initial fraction that enroll by 28 percentage points relative to a standard opt-in enrollment procedure.
items.b_text: Default savings behavior under automatic enrollment results in part from participant inertia.
items.explanation: Claim A quantifies the impact of active decision-making compared to standard opt-in enrollment, while Claim B identifies inertia as a mechanism underlying behavior under automatic enrollment defaults.

items.a_text: In the lab study, shelf display location (top versus bottom) had no significant effect on healthy snack choice.
items.b_text: The two studies that found no significant effect of positional changes on snack choice manipulated only minor order changes within arm's reach.
items.explanation: Claim A reports a null finding regarding vertical shelf placement on snack choice, while Claim B provides a descriptive characterization of studies that found no positional effect without directly reinforcing or contradicting the specific finding.

items.a_text: Compelling new hires to make active decisions about 401(k) enrollment raises the initial fraction that enroll by 28 percentage points relative to a standard opt-in enrollment procedure.
items.b_text: A substantial fraction of 401(k) participants hired under automatic enrollment retain the default fund allocation.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the impact of active choice mandates on initial 401(k) enrollment rates, whereas Claim B focuses on the stickiness of default fund allocations under automatic enrollment.

items.a_text: The majority of experimental studies examining choice architecture in self-service eating settings were of very weak quality.
items.b_text: Studies of interventions to change diet-related behaviours comprise 70.2% of the identified choice architecture micro-environment evidence base.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the methodological quality of studies in self-service eating settings, whereas Claim B describes the proportion of diet-related interventions within the choice architecture literature.

items.a_text: Reference dependence can play a major role in the effectiveness of default effects.
items.b_text: Designating an option as the default increases the frequency with which it is chosen relative to non-default options.
items.explanation: Claim B asserts the existence of the default effect, whereas Claim A identifies an underlying psychological mechanism (reference dependence) without directly reinforcing or contradicting the behavioral outcome.

items.a_text: In the lab study, shelf display location (top versus bottom) had no significant effect on healthy snack choice.
items.b_text: Purchases of products classified as healthy during the visual condition did not differ significantly from the control condition.
items.explanation: The claims evaluate distinct choice architecture interventions (shelf height placement versus a visual prompt condition), so neither directly supports nor contradicts the other.

items.a_text: In the lab study, there was no significant interaction effect between shelf arrangement and assortment structure on healthy snack choice.
items.b_text: Purchases of products classified as healthy during the visual condition did not differ significantly from the control condition.
items.explanation: The claims evaluate null effects of different nudge interventions (interaction between shelf arrangement and assortment structure versus a visual condition against a control) on healthy food choices.

items.a_text: In the field study, snack display manipulations had no significant main or interactive effects on the sales of unhealthy snacks or total snacks.
items.b_text: Purchases of products classified as healthy during the visual condition did not differ significantly from the control condition.
items.explanation: The claims evaluate the effects of display or visual nudges on different product categories (unhealthy/total snacks versus healthy products), addressing distinct outcomes rather than reinforcing or contradicting each other.

items.a_text: There was no difference in the sales of healthy products between the nudge condition and the nudge plus disclosure condition.
items.b_text: Purchases of products classified as healthy during the visual condition did not differ significantly from the control condition.
items.explanation: The claims evaluate entirely different experimental comparisons (nudge versus nudge plus disclosure, compared to a visual nudge versus control), representing distinct interventions rather than a shared finding.
